title: Hashing
html:
A hash set or hash map answers “have I seen this value?” in O(1) on average. Almost every problem in this topic is an O(n²) double loop that collapses to O(n) once the inner loop is replaced by one hash lookup — and half of them use the same trick: prefix sums stored in a hash map.

Hashing (as a problem-solving tool) — replacing search with lookup. Instead of scanning for a value, you keep every value you have met in a hash table and ask the table. Average O(1) per insert / lookup / delete, O(n) extra space, and no ordering.

The containers you will reach for

NeedPythonC++JavaJavaScript

Watch out

Iteration order over a hash container is not the same across languages (C++ and Java make no promise at all). When an answer is a set of values, sort it before printing — every solution below that prints several keys does exactly that.

Two questions decide the whole design of a hashing solution:

What is the key?

The raw value (pair with sum), a running prefix sum (subarray with sum), or a derived value such as prefix(a) − prefix(b) (common span).

What do I store with it?

Nothing (a set), a count (frequency problems), or the first index where the key appeared (longest-subarray problems).

The prefix-sum + hash map pattern

Let prefix[j] = arr[0] + … + arr[j]. Then the sum of any subarray is a difference of two prefix sums:

sum(arr[i..j]) = prefix[j] − prefix[i−1]

So “is there a subarray ending at j with sum S?” becomes “did the value prefix[j] − S appear as an earlier prefix sum?” — a single hash lookup instead of an inner loop over every start i.

1
Seed the map with prefix = 0 at index −1
The empty prefix. It makes a subarray that starts at index 0 fall out of the same formula instead of needing a special case.
2
Walk left to right, updating prefix
One addition per element.
3
Look up prefix − S
Found at index k ⇒ arr[k+1..j] sums to S. For existence answer immediately; for longest take j − k; for count add the stored count.
4
Insert prefix only if it is new
Keeping the first index gives the longest subarray; a later duplicate would only shorten it.
Key point

Four problems below are this one template with a different S or a different array: subarray with 0 sum (S = 0), longest subarray with given sum, longest subarray with equal 0s and 1s (map 0 → −1, then S = 0) and longest common span of two binary arrays (use a[i] − b[i], then S = 0).

Intersection of two unsorted arrays

Example

Input: a = [10, 15, 20, 5, 20], b = [30, 5, 30, 80]
Output: 1
Input: a = [1, 2, 3, 2, 4, 5], b = [3, 4, 5, 6]
Output: 3

Count the distinct values that appear in both arrays. Duplicates inside one array (the two 20s, the two 30s) are counted once.

Naive: for each element of a, skip it if it already appeared earlier in a, otherwise scan b for it. Two nested scans per element.

Time O(m · (m + n))Space O(1)
Idea

Put the distinct elements of a into a set. Scan b: every element found in the set is a common value — count it and remove it from the set, so a repeated value in b cannot be counted twice. Each element is touched once.

Time O(m + n)Space O(m)
Key point

Building two sets and counting the elements of one that are in the other (len(set(a) & set(b)) in Python) is the same O(m + n) idea; the remove-on-hit version needs only one set and no second pass.

Union of two unsorted arrays

Example

Input: a = [15, 20, 5, 15], b = [15, 15, 15, 20, 10]
Output: 4
Input: a = [1, 2, 3, 2, 4, 5], b = [3, 4, 5, 6]
Output: 6

Count the distinct values present in at least one of the arrays. The naive way copies both into one array of m + n elements and, for each element, scans everything before it to see whether it is a repeat.

Time O((m + n)²)Space O(m + n)
Idea

A set is a union with duplicates removed. Insert every element of both arrays and read off its size.

Time O(m + n)Space O(m + n)
Key point

If the arrays were sorted, both union and intersection could be done with the two-pointer merge walk in O(m + n) time and O(1) space — the hash set is what buys you the same time on unsorted input.

Pair with given sum

Example

Input: arr = [3, 2, 8, 15, -18], sum = 17
Output: Yes (2 + 15)
Input: arr = [2, 1, 6, 3], sum = 6
Output: No

Does the array contain two different elements whose sum is x? The naive check tries every pair.

Time O(n²)Space O(1)
Idea

Walk the array once. Before inserting arr[i], ask the set whether its complement x − arr[i] has already been seen. Checking before inserting guarantees the two elements are at different positions — [3] with x = 6 correctly answers No.

Time O(n)Space O(n)
Pitfall

Inserting all elements first and then asking x − v in set for each v accepts an element paired with itself ([3], x = 6 → wrong Yes). Insert after the lookup, or store counts and demand two copies when x − v == v.

Subarray with 0 sum

Example

Input: arr = [1, 2, 3, 2, 4, 5]
Output: No
Input: arr = [-1, 4, -3, 5, 1]
Output: Yes (4 − 3 − 1 = 0 … [-1, 4, -3])
Input: arr = [4, -3, -1, 2]
Output: Yes

Is there a contiguous subarray whose elements sum to zero? The naive solution computes the sum of every (i, j) range.

Time O(n²)Space O(1)
Idea

First use of the prefix-sum pattern. A zero-sum subarray arr[i..j] exists exactly when two prefix sums are equal, prefix[i−1] == prefix[j] — or when some prefix[j] is itself 0 (the subarray starts at index 0). Keep every prefix sum in a set; the first repeat (or a 0) is the answer.

Time O(n)Space O(n)
Key point

Subarray with a given sum S is the same code with prefix − S looked up instead of prefix. Seeding the set with 0 is what replaces the separate if prefix == 0 test of the original notes.

Check for palindrome permutation

Example

Input: s = "geek"
Output: No
Input: s = "geegg"
Output: Yes (gegeg, eggge, …)
Input: s = "aab"
Output: Yes (aba)

Can the characters of s be rearranged into a palindrome? Generating every permutation and testing each one is hopeless beyond a handful of characters — n! candidates.

Time O(n! · n)Space O(n)
Idea

A palindrome pairs every character with its mirror, so each character must occur an even number of times — except the single middle character of an odd-length string. Count frequencies in a hash map; the answer is Yes iff at most one count is odd. (Even length ⇒ zero odd counts; odd length ⇒ exactly one — “at most one” covers both.)

Time O(n)Space O(k) for k distinct characters
Key point

For a fixed alphabet a 26- or 256-slot array beats the hash map; for an unbounded alphabet (Unicode) the map is the right tool. A bit-twiddling variant toggles bit c in an integer mask and checks mask & (mask − 1) == 0 at the end.

Longest subarray with given sum

Example

Input: arr = [5, 8, -4, -4, 9, -2, 2], sum = 0
Output: 3 ([8, -4, -4])
Input: arr = [3, 1, 0, 1, 8, 2, 3, 6], sum = 5
Output: 4 ([3, 1, 0, 1])
Input: arr = [8, 3, 7], sum = 15
Output: 0

Return the length of the longest contiguous subarray whose sum is exactly S (0 if none). Naive: start at every i, extend to every j, keep the longest hit.

Time O(n²)Space O(1)
Idea

Prefix-sum pattern, longest flavour. At index j, if prefix[j] − S was first seen at index k, then arr[k+1..j] sums to S and has length j − k. Store each prefix sum with the first index it appeared at and never overwrite it — the earliest start gives the longest subarray. Seeding the map with 0 → −1 handles subarrays that start at index 0 (prefix[j] == S gives length j + 1).

Time O(n)Space O(n)
Pitfall

Overwriting first[prefix] on every occurrence (or using first[prefix] = j unconditionally) gives the shortest subarray, not the longest. Also, the two-pointer sliding window only works for arrays without negative numbers — this array has them, so the hash map is required.

Longest subarray with equal 0s and 1s

Example

Input: arr = [1, 0, 0, 1, 0, 1, 1]
Output: 6 ([1, 0, 0, 1, 0, 1] or [0, 0, 1, 0, 1, 1])
Input: arr = [1, 1, 1, 0]
Output: 2
Input: arr = [0, 0, 1, 1, 0]
Output: 4

In a binary array, find the longest contiguous subarray with as many 0s as 1s. The naive version tracks a running +1 / −1 score from each start.

Time O(n²)Space O(1)
Idea

Treat every 0 as −1. A subarray with equal 0s and 1s is then exactly a subarray with sum 0 — the previous problem with S = 0. Only the first index of each prefix sum is kept.

Time O(n)Space O(n)
Pitfall

The original notes overwrote the input (arr[i] = -1) before scanning. Compute the ±1 on the fly instead — callers rarely expect their array to come back changed, and the test harness that prints the input afterwards will expose it.

Longest common span with same sum in two binary arrays

Example

Input: a = [0, 1, 0, 0, 0, 0], b = [1, 0, 1, 0, 0, 1]
Output: 4 (a[1..4] and b[1..4] both sum to 1)
Input: a = [0, 0, 0], b = [1, 1, 1]
Output: 0
Input: a = [0, 0, 1, 0], b = [1, 1, 1, 1]
Output: 1

Two binary arrays of the same length. Find the longest index range [i..j] such that a[i..j] and b[i..j] have the same sum. Naive: for every start, extend both running sums together.

Time O(n²)Space O(1)
Idea

sum(a[i..j]) == sum(b[i..j]) ⟺ sum((a − b)[i..j]) == 0. So build the difference d[i] = a[i] − b[i] (values −1, 0, 1) and find the longest subarray with sum 0 in it — the same prefix-sum code again.

Time O(n)Space O(n)
Key point

The difference array has only 2n + 1 possible prefix values (−n … n), so an array indexed by prefix + n can replace the hash map here — same O(n) but no hashing at all. Nothing in the method needs the arrays to be binary; it works for any two integer arrays.

Longest consecutive subsequence

Example

Input: arr = [1, 9, 3, 4, 2, 20]
Output: 4 (1, 2, 3, 4)
Input: arr = [8, 20, 7, 30]
Output: 2 (7, 8)
Input: arr = [20, 30, 40]
Output: 1

Find the length of the longest run of consecutive integers x, x+1, x+2, … whose members all appear in the array — in any order and possibly with duplicates. Sorting makes runs adjacent, which gives an O(n log n) solution.

Time O(n log n)Space O(n) for the sorted copy
Idea

Put everything in a set. A run x, x+1, … can only be counted from its start, and x is a start exactly when x − 1 is not in the set. For each start, walk upward while x + k is present. Every element is reached by at most one such walk, so the total work is O(n) even though there is a nested while.

Time O(n)Space O(n)
Pitfall

Without the x − 1 not in set test the inner while restarts from every element of a run and the algorithm degrades to O(n²) on [1, 2, 3, …, n]. The check is what makes each run be walked exactly once.

Count distinct elements in every window

Example

Input: arr = [10, 20, 20, 10, 30, 40, 10], k = 4
Output: 2 3 4 3
Input: arr = [10, 20, 30, 40], k = 3
Output: 3 3

For each of the n − k + 1 windows of size k, print the number of distinct values in it. The naive solution rebuilds a set for every window.

Time O(n · k)Space O(k)
Idea

Consecutive windows differ by one element on each side. Keep a count map of the current window: when the window slides, decrement the outgoing element (delete the key when its count hits 0) and increment the incoming one. The number of keys in the map is the answer for that window — maintained in O(1) per slide.

Time O(n)Space O(k)
Pitfall

Forgetting to delete a key whose count reached 0 makes len(count) too large — the map still “remembers” a value that left the window. Python's Counter has the same trap: c[x] -= 1 leaves a zero entry behind.

Elements appearing more than n/k times

Example

Input: arr = [30, 10, 20, 20, 10, 20, 30, 30], k = 4
Output: 20 30 (n/k = 2; 20 and 30 appear 3 times)
Input: arr = [2, 2, 1, 2, 3, 2], k = 2
Output: 2 (the majority element)

Print every value that occurs strictly more than n / k times (n / k with integer division). k = 2 is the classic majority element. Sorting groups equal values together, so a single pass can count runs:

Time O(n log n)Space O(1) extra (in-place sort)
Idea

Hash map of counts. One pass to count, one pass over the map to report keys with count > n / k. The result is sorted before printing because map order is not portable.

Time O(n)Space O(n)

Space-efficient method — O(nk) time, O(k) space. At most k − 1 values can appear more than n / k times (if k of them did, they would add up to more than n elements). So it is enough to track k − 1 candidates, in the style of the Boyer–Moore majority vote:

1
Candidate seen again
If arr[i] is already a candidate, increment its count.
2
Room for a new candidate
If fewer than k − 1 candidates are stored, add arr[i] with count 1.
3
Table full
Otherwise decrement every candidate's count and drop the ones that reach 0. This “cancels” k distinct values at once — the k − 1 candidates and arr[i].
4
Verify
A value with more than n / k occurrences cannot be cancelled away (each cancellation round consumes k distinct elements, so there are fewer than n / k rounds), but a survivor is not guaranteed to be frequent. Recount the real occurrences of each survivor in a second pass and keep those above n / k.
Time O(n · k)Space O(k)
Pitfall

Skipping the second pass is the classic error: the candidate table can hold values that are not frequent (every element of [1, 2, 3, 4] with k = 4 survives the first pass, yet none appears more than once). Candidates are only possible answers.

Interview Q&A

Why do the “longest subarray” problems store the first index of each prefix sum, while “subarray exists” only needs a set?

Existence needs one bit of information: has this prefix sum appeared? Longest needs where did it first appear? — the earliest index gives the longest span ending at the current position, so the map must never overwrite an existing key. A third variant, count the subarrays with sum S, stores how many times each prefix sum appeared and adds that count at every step.

What is the worst-case time of these solutions, and does it matter?

Hash table operations are O(1) on average but O(n) in the worst case (all keys collide), so every “O(n)” above is really expected time. With the built-in hash functions and random-looking data this never bites; in adversarial settings (competitive programming hacks, untrusted input) use a randomised hash or fall back to sorting (O(n log n) guaranteed).

When would you choose sorting over hashing for these problems?

When memory is tight (sorting can be in place, a hash table costs O(n) extra), when you need the output in order anyway, or when the keys are hard to hash (floating point, large composite objects). Union/intersection of arrays that are already sorted are O(m + n) with two pointers and need no hash table at all.

The 0/1 subarray problem and the common-span problem look different from “subarray with sum 0” — how do you spot the reduction?

Ask what equal counts means arithmetically: equal 0s and 1s ⇔ Σ(+1 for 1, −1 for 0) = 0; equal sums in a and b ⇔ Σ(a[i] − b[i]) = 0. Whenever a condition can be written as some derived array sums to 0 (or to S) over a range, the prefix-sum + hash map template applies unchanged.

Explain why the n/k candidate method needs only k − 1 slots.

If k different values each appeared more than n / k times, together they would account for more than n elements, which is impossible. Hence at most k − 1 values can qualify, and a table of k − 1 counters suffices to track every possible answer — the same argument that gives the single counter of Boyer–Moore majority voting for k = 2.
